newsitem.title: USA: Jury begins deliberating Megan's Law case.
newsitem.headline: Jury begins deliberating Megan's Law case.

text.p: Jury deliberations began Thursday in the murder trial of a New Jersey man charged with raping and strangling 7-year-old Megan Kanka, a crime that inspired the so-called Megan's Law.

The jury of seven women and five men received two hours of instructions from Mercer County Superior Court Judge Andrew Smithson before beginning their deliberations on an eight count indictment against Jesse Timmendequas, 36.
If convicted, he faces the possiblity of the death penalty.
Timmendequas is accused of luring the girl to the bedroom of his house in Hamilton Township, New Jersey, July 29, 1994, to see a puppy and then attacking and killing her.
Final arguments ended on Wednesday with the prosecution portraying the defendant as a calculating killer and the defence saying he took the blame for an accidential slaying.
Prosecutor Kathryn Flicker described in ghastly detail how Timmendequas lured the girl into his home, raped and strangled her and later dumped her body in a park.
Timmendequas' defence attorney, Barbara Lependorf, in a three-hour summation said the defendant was a victim and suggested he was protecting one or both of his roommates.
Timmendequas lived with two other men across the street from the Kanka family. He confessed to the crimes and led police to the body.
The crime sparked a public outcry because the girl's parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka, had not known that Timmendequas was a sex offender twice convicted in assaults involving girls aged 7 and 5.

Megan's Law was the result of the family's impassioned campaigning. Originally the law required sex offenders to register with authorities and empowered authorities to notify the public about those they regarded as posing the highest risk.

But a series of rulings left the state with the power to require registration but not to notify the public and that aspect of the law is being challenged in federal court. Critics say Megan's Law violates the Constitution by punishing criminals after they have served out their sentences.
Most other states have similar laws and in 1996 President Clinton signed a law making it easier for residents to get information about released sex offenders.
